title: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves

learn.hook: A brand-new delivery van bought for ₹8 lakh will not be worth ₹8 lakh after five years of Mumbai traffic. Accounting must recognise that steady decline. That is depreciation.
points: Depreciation is the decline in the value of a fixed (depreciable) asset due to use, passage of time or obsolescence. It is the allocation of the asset's cost over its useful life.

Features: it reduces the book value of the asset; it is a non-cash expense (no cash goes out when it is charged); it is a continuing process over the asset's life; it applies to fixed assets only, not to current assets like stock.
Depreciation is charged to the profit and loss account as an expense of each year of use.
Land is not depreciated, because it normally has an unlimited useful life and does not get used up. Buildings on the land are depreciated.

example.q: A firm buys a machine for ₹5,00,000 with a 10-year life and no scrap value. How much depreciation is charged per year, and is cash paid each year?
steps: This amount is charged to the P&L account every year.
No cash goes out when depreciation is charged; the cash was paid when the machine was bought.
example.answer: ₹50,000 a year; it is a non-cash expense.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways depreciates its coaches and locomotives over decades of service, but not the land under its stations.

topics.title: Depletion, amortisation and causes of depreciation

learn.hook: Coal India mines coal, a pharma company holds a 20-year patent, and a call centre buys computers. All three lose asset value, but accountants use three different words for it.
points: Depletion: reduction in the value of wasting (natural) assets such as mines, quarries and oil wells, as the resources are extracted. It is usually based on the quantity extracted.
Amortisation: writing off the cost of intangible assets such as patents, copyrights, trademarks and goodwill over their useful life.

Causes of depreciation: (1) wear and tear due to use or passage of time; (2) expiration of legal rights (leases, patents, copyrights); (3) obsolescence, when an asset becomes outdated because of new technology or changes in demand; (4) abnormal factors such as accidents, fire, flood or earthquake.
Depletion is calculated by: (Cost ÷ Total estimated quantity) × Quantity extracted in the year.

example.q: A mine costing ₹50,00,000 is estimated to contain 1,00,000 tonnes of ore. 8,000 tonnes are extracted this year. Find depletion.

learn.reallife: When smartphones replaced feature phones, many Indian factories making keypad phones saw their machines become obsolete long before they physically wore out.

topics.title: Need for depreciation and factors in measuring it

learn.hook: If a taxi owner ignored the wearing out of his cab, he'd think he was richer every year, until the day the cab died and he had no money for a new one.
points: Need: (1) matching the cost of the asset with the revenue it helps earn, for correct profit; (2) tax: depreciation is an allowable deduction for income tax; (3) true and fair financial position: assets are not overstated; (4) compliance with law (the Companies Act requires it); (5) retaining funds for replacement, since profit available for distribution is reduced.
Cost of asset (depreciable cost base): purchase price plus all costs to bring it to working condition: freight, cartage, installation, commission, registration.
Estimated net residual (scrap) value: expected sale value at the end of its life, less disposal costs.
Estimated useful life: the period (or production units) over which the asset is expected to be used.
Depreciable amount = Cost − Net residual value.

example.q: A machine is bought for ₹4,50,000; freight ₹15,000; installation ₹35,000. Estimated scrap ₹50,000; life 9 years. Find the depreciable amount and annual depreciation (equal instalments).

learn.reallife: An app-cab fleet owner in Hyderabad sets aside the depreciation amount every year so that when the cars wear out, the business can afford new ones.

learn.hook: Under the straight line method, depreciation is the same every year, like a fixed monthly SIP. Plot the book value on a graph and you get a straight line sloping down.
points: Straight line (fixed instalment or original cost) method: equal depreciation every year. Annual depreciation = (Cost − Net residual value) ÷ Estimated useful life.
Rate of depreciation under SLM = (Annual depreciation ÷ Cost) × 100. Depreciation can also be found as Cost × Rate ÷ 100.
Advantages: simple to calculate; the asset can be written down to zero (or scrap value) at the end of its life; suitable where use is even across years.

Limitations: ignores the fact that repairs rise as assets age, so the total charge (depreciation + repairs) rises in later years; does not consider the effective use of the asset; interest on capital invested is ignored.
Suitable for: patents, copyrights, leases and furniture, i.e. assets whose usefulness falls evenly with time.

example.q: Cost ₹1,60,000; scrap ₹10,000; life 5 years. Find annual depreciation, the rate, and book value after 2 years.

learn.reallife: A coaching institute in Kota writes off its classroom furniture and its 10-year lease equally each year: the straight line method suits both.

topics.title: Written down value method (WDV) and comparison with SLM

learn.hook: Under WDV, depreciation is big in the early years and shrinks later, much like a new phone that loses the most value in its first year.
points: Written down value (reducing or diminishing balance) method: a fixed rate is applied to the opening book value each year. Depreciation falls every year.
Under WDV the book value never reaches zero.

Advantages: total charge (depreciation + repairs) stays fairly even, since high depreciation in early years meets low repairs, and vice versa; accepted by income tax authorities; suitable where obsolescence is fast.
Limitations: the asset cannot be fully written off; finding a suitable rate is difficult; calculations are more involved.

Comparison: SLM charges on original cost, equal amounts, book value can become zero, suits patents, leases, furniture. WDV charges on reducing book value, decreasing amounts, never zero, suits plant, machinery, vehicles, and is recognised by income tax law.

example.q: Machine cost ₹2,00,000; WDV rate 20%. Find depreciation for 3 years and the book value at the end of year 3.

learn.reallife: Income tax rules in India prescribe WDV rates for blocks of assets; for example, vehicles and computers are grouped into blocks with their own rates.

topics.title: Depreciation for part of a year, additions and repairs

learn.hook: Buy a machine on 1 October and close books on 31 March, and it has worked for you for exactly six months. Depreciation must count those months, not the full year.
points: When an asset is bought during the year, depreciation is charged from the date of purchase to the end of the year: Depreciation = Cost × Rate × Months used ÷ 12 (under SLM; under WDV, on the book value).
Count months carefully: bought 1 July, year ending 31 March: July to March = 9 months. Bought 1 January: 3 months.
If a question says the rate is 'per annum', time is always prorated; if it says depreciation is charged for a full year regardless, follow the instruction.
Additions or extensions that increase capacity or life (a new wing, an extra unit) are capitalised and depreciated separately from their date of addition.
Ordinary repairs and maintenance that only keep an asset working are revenue expenses, charged to P&L; they are not added to the asset.

example.q: On 1 April 2025 a firm has machinery ₹4,00,000. On 1 October 2025 it adds a machine for ₹1,20,000. Depreciation 10% p.a. SLM; year ends 31 March 2026. Find depreciation for 2025-26.

topics.title: Recording depreciation: asset account vs provision for depreciation

learn.hook: Two firms buy the same ₹1,00,000 machine. After 3 years, one balance sheet shows 'Machinery ₹70,000'; the other shows 'Machinery ₹1,00,000 less Provision ₹30,000'. Same truth, two styles.
points: Method 1: charging depreciation to the asset account. Entries: Dr Depreciation / Cr Asset; then Dr P&L / Cr Depreciation. The asset account shows the reduced book value each year.

Method 2: creating a provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) account. Entries: Dr Depreciation / Cr Provision for Depreciation; then Dr P&L / Cr Depreciation. The asset stays at original cost.
Balance sheet (method 1): asset at written down value. Balance sheet (method 2): asset at cost, less provision for depreciation (accumulated), showing net book value.
Advantage of method 2: original cost and total depreciation to date are both visible at a glance, which helps for insurance, tax and replacement decisions.

example.q: Machine bought 1 April 2023 for ₹1,00,000; SLM 10% p.a. Show the balance sheet position on 31 March 2026 under both methods.
steps: Method 2: Machinery ₹1,00,000 less Provision for depreciation ₹30,000 = ₹70,000.
example.answer: ₹70,000 net under both; method 2 also shows cost ₹1,00,000 and accumulated depreciation ₹30,000.

learn.reallife: Schedule III statements of companies like Bajaj Auto show gross block, accumulated depreciation and net block for each class of asset, which is method 2 in action.

topics.title: Disposal of an asset: book value, profit or loss, disposal account

learn.hook: Selling an old machine is like selling a used bike: whether you 'profit' depends on what it's worth in your books today, not what you paid for it years ago.
points: Steps: find the book value on the date of sale (cost less depreciation up to that date, including depreciation for the part of the year before sale).
Profit on sale = Sale price − Book value (credited to P&L). Loss on sale = Book value − Sale price (debited to P&L).
Entries (asset account method): Dr Depreciation / Cr Asset (for the part year); Dr Bank / Cr Asset (sale proceeds); for profit Dr Asset / Cr P&L; for loss Dr P&L / Cr Asset.

Asset disposal account: transfer the asset's cost (Dr Disposal / Cr Asset), its accumulated depreciation (Dr Provision / Cr Disposal) and sale proceeds (Dr Bank / Cr Disposal); the balance is profit or loss, transferred to P&L.
Partial sale: only the part sold is removed with its depreciation; the remaining assets continue to be depreciated in full.

example.q: Machine bought 1 April 2023 for ₹1,00,000; SLM 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March. Sold on 1 October 2025 for ₹70,000. Find profit or loss.

learn.reallife: When State Transport Corporations auction old buses, each sale is compared with the bus's book value to decide profit or loss on disposal.

topics.title: Disposal with provision for depreciation and insurance claims

learn.hook: When a fire destroys a machine, the insurer pays only part of its value. Accounting must show three things: the depreciation written back, the claim and the loss that's left.
points: When a provision for depreciation account is kept, the accumulated depreciation on the asset sold is transferred: Dr Provision for Depreciation / Cr Asset (or Cr Asset Disposal).
The asset account is then credited with sale proceeds and the balance is profit or loss, or all items are collected in an asset disposal account.

Asset destroyed by fire or accident: find book value on that date. Insurance claim admitted: Dr Insurance Claim (or Insurance Company) / Cr Asset (or Disposal). Uncovered loss: Dr Loss by Fire (to P&L) / Cr Asset.
Loss by fire = Book value on the date of fire − Insurance claim admitted (− any scrap value realised).

example.q: Machine cost ₹2,00,000; accumulated depreciation ₹80,000. Destroyed by fire; insurer admits ₹90,000. Find the loss and pass the entries (provision method).
steps: Dr Provision for Depreciation ₹80,000 / Cr Machinery ₹80,000.
Loss = 1,20,000 − 90,000 = ₹30,000: Dr Loss by Fire (P&L) / Cr Machinery ₹30,000.

learn.reallife: After a cyclone hits Odisha's coast, factories that insured their plants record insurance claims for the book value lost, and only the uninsured part hits profit.

topics.title: Provisions and the provision for doubtful debts

learn.hook: Some customers who owe you money will never pay. You don't know who yet, but experience says about 5%. A provision lets you face that loss before it hits.
points: A provision is an amount charged against profit to provide for a known liability or a likely loss whose amount cannot be determined with certainty.
Examples: provision for depreciation, provision for bad and doubtful debts, provision for taxation, provision for repairs and renewals, provision for discount on debtors.
Bad debts written off: Dr Bad Debts / Cr Debtor; then Dr P&L / Cr Bad Debts. Creating a provision: Dr P&L / Cr Provision for Doubtful Debts.

When a provision already exists, bad debts are transferred to it: Dr Provision for Doubtful Debts / Cr Bad Debts. The charge to P&L = Bad debts + New provision − Old provision. If negative, the excess is credited to P&L.
New provision is calculated on debtors after deducting further bad debts. In the balance sheet: Debtors less Provision.

example.q: Debtors ₹2,00,000; further bad debts ₹10,000; new provision 5%; old provision ₹6,000; bad debts during the year ₹4,000. Find the P&L charge.
steps: Debtors after further bad debts = ₹1,90,000; new provision = 5% = ₹9,500.

learn.reallife: RBI requires banks to make provisions on loans that turn doubtful; that is why bank results in India report 'provisions' as a separate charge against profit.

topics.title: Reserves and how they differ from provisions

learn.hook: A provision is like an umbrella you must buy because rain is forecast. A reserve is like extra savings you choose to keep from your pocket money, just in case.
points: A reserve is an amount set aside out of profit (an appropriation of profit) to strengthen the financial position, meet contingencies or for specific purposes. It is created after profit is ascertained.
Provision is a charge against profit; reserve is an appropriation of profit.
Provision is made for a known liability or expected loss; reserve is made to strengthen the business or meet future needs, with no specific liability in mind (except specific reserves).
Provision is shown as a deduction from the related asset or under liabilities; reserve is shown under 'Reserves and Surplus' on the liabilities side.
Provision must be made even if there is a loss; reserve is created only when there is profit. Provisions cannot be used for dividend; some revenue reserves can be.

example.q: Net profit ₹5,00,000 after charging provision for doubtful debts ₹20,000. The owner transfers ₹50,000 to general reserve. Which is a charge and which is an appropriation?
steps: Provision ₹20,000 was deducted to arrive at profit: a charge against profit.
₹50,000 transferred out of profit after it was ascertained: an appropriation of profit.
example.answer: Provision: charge against profit; reserve: appropriation of profit.

learn.reallife: Banks like SBI transfer a part of their profits to statutory reserves each year: an appropriation that strengthens their capital base.

topics.title: Types of reserves and secret reserves

learn.hook: Some reserves come from everyday trading profit, some from rare capital gains, and some are hidden from view altogether. Each has a different job.
points: Revenue reserves are created out of revenue (trading) profits, e.g. general reserve, dividend equalisation reserve. They can be used for any purpose, including dividends.

Capital reserves are created out of capital profits, e.g. premium on issue of shares or debentures, profit on sale of fixed assets, profit on reissue of forfeited shares, profit prior to incorporation, profit on revaluation of assets. They are generally not available for dividends and are used to write off capital losses.

General reserve: not for any specific purpose. Specific reserves: for a stated purpose, e.g. dividend equalisation reserve, debenture redemption reserve, workmen compensation fund, investment fluctuation fund.
Importance of reserves: meet unforeseen losses, strengthen financial position, help expansion, stabilise dividends, redeem long-term liabilities.

Secret reserve: a reserve not shown in the balance sheet, created by undervaluing assets or overstating liabilities, e.g. excessive depreciation, undervaluing stock, excessive provision for doubtful debts, charging capital expenditure to revenue. Merits: hides fluctuations and strengthens position. Demerits: hides true profit and position, can be misused, and goes against full disclosure and the requirement of a true and fair view.

example.q: A firm charges depreciation at 25% on a machine when 10% is reasonable. Machine cost ₹4,00,000. What secret reserve is created in year 1 (SLM basis)?
steps: Excess = 1,00,000 − 40,000 = ₹60,000: profit is understated and the asset undervalued by this amount.

learn.reallife: Banks and insurers in India must disclose their reserves clearly; hidden cushions are discouraged because depositors and policyholders rely on true accounts.
